analysis.one_liner: Requires health care and social service employers to adopt workplace violence prevention plans and training.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a vote: after its introduction it was referred to the Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee, which took no action before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: Health care and social service workers face among the highest rates of on-the-job violence of any occupation, often from patients, clients, or visitors. This bill would have required the Department of Labor to issue a binding safety standard, built on OSHA's 2015 voluntary guidelines, forcing hospitals, nursing homes, group homes, home health agencies, and similar employers to write and maintain workplace violence prevention plans. Those plans would have to include risk assessments done with frontline employees, hazard fixes like alarms and security staffing, annual training, incident logs, and anti-retaliation protections. Hospitals and nursing homes not covered by OSHA — including many state-government-run facilities — would have had to comply as a condition of participating in Medicare.
analysis.who_benefits: Roughly the health care and social service workforce: nurses, aides, orderlies, emergency responders, social workers, and home health workers. They would gain enforceable prevention plans, annual training, incident reporting and investigation, hazard corrections such as alarms and staffing controls, and protection from being retaliated against for reporting violence. Patients would also benefit indirectly, since de-escalation training and safer staffing arrangements reduce the confrontations that harm both sides.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Nurses, aides, social and home care workers

how_it_helps.text: Requires each covered employer to develop a written workplace violence prevention plan with meaningful participation of direct care employees, tailored to each facility and service, including patient-specific and environmental risk factors.

Mandates hazard controls using the hierarchy of controls — such as alarm systems, access controls, barrier protection, staffing and team assignments, and flagging clients with a history of violence — with timely correction of hazards found in investigations.

Requires violent incident investigation, a violent incident log kept for at least 5 years, annual training appropriate to workers' language and literacy, and annual evaluation of the plan's effectiveness.
Prohibits employers from retaliating against employees who report workplace violence incidents, threats, or concerns, enforced like any OSHA standard.
Extends compliance to certain hospitals and skilled nursing facilities not otherwise covered by OSHA by conditioning their Medicare participation on meeting the standard.

analysis.who_pays: Covered employers — hospitals, nursing homes, hospice and home health agencies, group homes, psychiatric and substance-use treatment centers, emergency services, and their contractors — would bear the cost of risk assessments, written plans, engineering controls, security staffing, training, and recordkeeping. Some of that cost could flow to patients and payers through higher prices, and employers would face OSHA enforcement if they failed to comply.

drawbacks.text: Compliance costs fall on facilities that are often already financially strained, including nursing homes and rural hospitals, and could be passed on through higher prices or reduced services.

The bill lets the interim standard bypass normal OSHA rulemaking procedures, including some review requirements, in favor of a 30-day public comment period; critics of expedited rulemaking would object to the speed.
Some controls, like staffing levels and dedicated security personnel, impose judgments on employers about operational choices that they would argue are better left to management.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For the workers who face beatings, threats, and psychological trauma on the job — some of the most common victims of workplace violence in the economy — the protections are substantial and the cost is a compliance burden on employers. The honest objections are about cost pressure on already-tight facilities and the speed of rulemaking, not about whether the workers are genuinely exposed. On balance, the bill's benefits to a large, mostly female and low-wage workforce outweigh those costs, though the paperwork and enforcement burden is real.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to the Senate health committee, which never took it up, and it expired when the two-year Congress ended in January 2025.

narrative.text: Sen. Tammy Baldwin introduced the bill on April 18, 2023, with 22 original Senate cosponsors.
The same day, the Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions.
The bill finished with 37 cosponsors — 36 of the Senate's 48 Democrats and 1 of the 4 Independents — and no Republican support.
No further action was ever recorded; the committee never reported the bill, and it died at the end of the 118th Congress.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Covered employers — hospitals, nursing homes, and home and social service providers — are better off, because they avoid the compliance costs of prevention plans, training, hazard controls, and recordkeeping. Health care workers continue to work without a federal violence-prevention standard.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Health care employers who avoid compliance costs

for.name: Sen. Tammy Baldwin
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and recruited 22 original cosponsors.

for.name: 36 of 48 Senate Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, giving it a large majority of the Democratic caucus.

against.name: Senate HELP Committee
against.role: Committee of referral; took no action
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral on April 18, 2023 and never reported it out, keeping it from the Senate floor for the rest of the Congress.

against.name: Senate Republicans
against.what_they_did: No Republican senator cosponsored the bill, leaving it without the bipartisan support needed to advance in the chamber.

sides.party_line_note: All 37 cosponsors were Democrats or the chamber's Independents; no Republican signed on, and the committee chaired by the majority took no action.

industries.note: Hospitals would have had to fund prevention plans, engineering controls like alarms and weapon detectors, training, and incident logs, and face OSHA enforcement — and many hospitals not covered by OSHA would have had to comply as a condition of Medicare participation. Safer conditions would have protected their workforces, but the industry's interest in minimizing compliance costs ran against the workers' interest in enforceable standards.

industries.industry: Nursing homes and long-term care facilities
industries.note: Nursing homes, hospice, and memory care facilities are covered facilities and would bear the same plan, training, and recordkeeping requirements on thin margins; their staff are among the most frequently assaulted workers. The bill would have benefited their workers at the facilities' expense.

industries.industry: Home health and social service agencies
industries.note: Home health, home-based hospice, and home-based social work are covered services, so agencies and contractors would have needed plans, training, and coordination procedures for field workers; their interest in low overhead ran against their employees' interest in protection in isolated settings.
